channel.title: Said & Checked: Transportation and Infrastructure — AskAmerica
channel.description: What officeholders said each day about Transportation and Infrastructure, and which statements government data supports, contradicts or rules out.

item.title: Said & Checked, Transportation and Infrastructure, 2026-11-20: none false or contradicted, 1 unsupported, 3 unsettled (Sheldon Whitehouse, Chuck Grassley)
item.description:
No statement was found false or contradicted.

Unsupported and Unsettled

  • Sheldon Whitehouse, U.S. Senator: “in Rhode Island, the NEPA environmental review process was estimated to add thousands of dollars to the cost of each replacement bus shelter.” Unsupported. No source documenting a per-shelter NEPA cost in Rhode Island was found; the search covered the warehouse catalog, web searches and ecoRI's reporting on RIPTA shelters, and RIPTA's board packet refused the fetch.
  • Chuck Grassley, U.S. Senator: “there is a road in Colorado that took 13 years to build due to Federal permitting delays; another project in Wyoming, a wind project, that waited 12 years for Federal approval; and a mine in Minnesota that took 12 years…” Unsettled. A Colorado Politics op-ed says Interstate 70's expansion took 13 years of environmental review before work began, and the Permitting Council's page for the Chokecherry and Sierra Madre wind project in Wyoming shows it proposed in 2008 with a federal decision in 2012 and later phase approvals; neither project was confirmed as the one meant, and the 12-year wait is not established.
  • Sheldon Whitehouse, U.S. Senator: “Rather than wait 5 or 10 years to get a bridge or tunnel permitted, BAAJA will reduce those timelines to a little over 2 years.” Unsettled. The bill sets a 2-year deadline for environmental impact statements, but CEQ's January 2025 report puts the median recent statement at 2.2 to 2.8 years, with a quarter taking more than six years, and existing law already sets a 2-year deadline, so the 5-to-10-year premise fits only slower cases.

item.title: Said & Checked, Transportation and Infrastructure, 2026-11-19: 1 contradicted (Markwayne Mullin)
item.description:
False or contradicted

  • Markwayne Mullin, Secretary of Homeland Security: “We landed over 4,000 planes when the ground stoppage went out because of the communication and didn't have one single incident.” Contradicted. The FAA's Nov. 15 Q&A says "approximately 3,500 aircraft safely landed" when the ground stop was implemented, below the more than 4,000 stated, and that every passenger arrived safely. The FAA figure is approximate, and the FAA and L3Harris investigation into the root cause is still open.

Disagreements

  • Markwayne Mullin, Secretary of Homeland Security: “If we canceled something with the airspace completely open, it could bring confusion” (premise supported)
    Bennie Thompson, U.S. Representative from Mississippi: “For the secretary of homeland security to do that during a crisis was not only irresponsible, Mr. Secretary, but also incredibly tone-deaf.”
    Both statements in context

item.title: Said & Checked, Transportation and Infrastructure, 2026-11-18: none false or contradicted, 6 unsettled (Sean Duffy, Suhas Subramanyam)
item.description:
No statement was found false or contradicted.

Unsettled

  • Sean Duffy, Secretary of Transportation: “Reported as: He again reiterated that it is was a faulty router made by Juniper Networks that was to blame.” Unsettled. The FAA's Nov. 15 Q&A traces the Nov. 13 ground stop to a flood of connection attempts from two sites, Amarillo, Texas, and El Dorado, Arkansas, where L3Harris was deploying a new router. It says the FAA and L3Harris are still investigating the root cause and does not name Juniper or call a router faulty. AskAmerica's FAA advisory data show the nationwide ground stop issued Nov. 13 but carry no cause.
  • Suhas Subramanyam, U.S. Representative from Virginia: “Rather than take responsibility, Secretary Duffy was quick to blame Congress, while also asking for an additional $50 billion.” Unsettled. Duffy did call for $50 billion at the Nov. 13 briefing. He attributed the outage to legacy equipment and a contractor, and on Meet the Press said 'I can't blame Republicans or Democrats, because it's all of them'. Whether that counts as blaming Congress depends on how it is read. Duffy's words are as reported by Fox 4 and Wichita Liberty.
  • Suhas Subramanyam, U.S. Representative from Virginia: “They have only spent $1 billion of those dollars. Nearly all of it has gone unspent” Unsettled. No published outlay figure for the $12.5 billion was found. GAO reports $1.8 billion obligated (20% of the $9 billion systems money) as of March 2026, which counts commitments, not spending. AskAmerica's USAspending data show FY2026 gross outlays of $1.416 billion for the FAA Facilities and Equipment account as a whole, which mixes in other funds.

Disagreements

  • Sean Duffy, Secretary of Transportation: “Reported as: He again reiterated that it is was a faulty router made by Juniper Networks that was to blame.” (unsettled)
    Suhas Subramanyam, U.S. Representative from Virginia: “the FAA problem that occurred on Friday was actually a configuration issue.” (unsettled)
    Both statements in context

item.title: Said & Checked, Transportation and Infrastructure, 2026-11-17: none false or contradicted, 2 unsupported, 4 unsettled (Donald Trump, Sean Duffy)
item.description:
No statement was found false or contradicted.

Unsupported and Unsettled

  • Donald Trump, President of the United States: “But we had 18 broken windows.” Unsupported. No official or independent account of 18 broken White House windows was found; the only sources for the figure are reports of this remark. The search covered AskAmerica's catalog (no table on White House building condition), the reporting story and news coverage; no White House, National Park Service or Secret Service record of window damage was found or read.
  • Sean Duffy, Secretary of Transportation: “I can't build new software to manage our airplanes in the airspace because it dates back to the 1990s.” Unsupported. No official account read directly dates the FAA's core air traffic management software to the 1990s; the FAA's ground-stop Q&A and its new-system fact sheet do not give its age. The search covered those two FAA pages and web searches; DOT's modernization plan, reportedly referring to 1990s automation platforms, could not be read (access refused), and DOT inspector general and GAO reports were not read.
  • Donald Trump, President of the United States: “Essentially, what you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack.” Unsettled. The FAA's Nov. 15 account names both causes: it says the FAA's legacy equipment 'became unstable' and also names a router installed by contractor L3Harris at El Dorado, Ark., as one of two likely sources of the data flood. Its root-cause investigation with L3Harris is still open.

Disagreements

  • Sean Duffy, Secretary of Transportation: “I have no money in that $12.5 billion that I can use for a new architecture for telecom.” (unsettled)
    Jim Himes, U.S. Representative from Connecticut: “that's sitting in your bank account right now?” (premise unsettled)
    Both statements in context

item.title: Said & Checked, Transportation and Infrastructure, 2026-11-16: none false or contradicted, 2 unsettled (Donald Trump)
item.description:
No statement was found false or contradicted.

Unsettled

  • Donald Trump, President of the United States: “It is in a terrible state of disrepair, as anybody can see by just looking at the pictures that are now circulating all over the Country, and in the Court” Unsettled. FOX 5 DC reports that a court filing by the superintendent of the National Mall and Memorial Parks says the former operator did not keep up agreed maintenance and found several areas of the course "to either be deteriorating or needing work". The filing itself could not be read directly, and no National Park Service condition assessment or deferred-maintenance figure for the course was found. Whether that amounts to a "terrible state of disrepair" is a judgment the record read does not settle.
  • Donald Trump, President of the United States: “They don't call it Trash Island for no reason!” Unsettled. City Cast DC reports that, according to an Oct. 9 Washington Post story, National Park Service crews had used the name for "an overgrown central area of debris and invasive vegetation" in the park; that Post story could not be read directly. City Cast also reports that the D.C. Public Library's People's Archive "did not find a record where East Potomac Park had been referred to as 'Trash Island'" and that a search of the Post's archive found no earlier use of the name for the park. Only the name was checked.

item.title: Said & Checked, Transportation and Infrastructure, 2026-11-15: 2 contradicted (Sean Duffy)
item.description:
False or contradicted

  • Sean Duffy, U.S. Secretary of Transportation: “Reported as: He has said the problem began when L3Harris was replacing a section of old copper wire with new fiber wire, somehow causing the system to overload.” Contradicted. The FAA's published account says otherwise. Asked whether upgrades caused the outage, it answers no and attributes the instability to the legacy system. It says data from two sites, a radar site in Amarillo, Texas and a radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas, where L3Harris had deployed a new router, flooded the network. The FAA also says the root cause is still under investigation, and L3Harris has not named a cause. The wording checked is AP's account of what the secretary said.
  • Sean Duffy, U.S. Secretary of Transportation: “They gave me money for tower -- for radios, money for radar, money for systems. But I don't have any money in that $12.5 billion for a new architecture for telecom.” Contradicted. Section 40003(a)(1) of Public Law 119-21 appropriates $4,750,000,000 "for telecommunications infrastructure modernization and systems upgrades", the largest single item in the $12.5 billion. Still open: whether that item can pay for a wholly new telecommunications architecture, as distinct from upgrades; the law's text does not say.

Contradictions and Disagreements

  • Contradicts own statement.
    Sean Duffy, U.S. Secretary of Transportation: “So we were forced by the telecom provider to actually update that copper to fiber, and we brought in our routers and did the work.” (unsettled)
    Sean Duffy, U.S. Secretary of Transportation: “There was an old fiber line that was going to be decommissioned by our telecom provider.” (unsettled)
    Both statements in context
  • Donald Trump, President of the United States: “old and broken system worse than when they began”
    Sean Duffy, U.S. Secretary of Transportation: “And I can't blame Republicans or Democrats, because it's all of them.” (premise supported)
    Both statements in context
  • Sean Duffy, U.S. Secretary of Transportation: “So all that money hasn't been spent, but it's been obligated to radar.” (unsettled)
    Jim Himes, U.S. Representative from Connecticut: “This is not a Congress money problem. You pointed out that there was $50 billion sent in the Biden administration and $12.5 billion appropriated that has not been obligated.” (unsettled)
    Both statements in context
